title: How to Facilitate a Blameless Postmortem
author: Gustavo Razzetti
summary: Gustavo Razzetti explains how leaders can replace blame with curiosity when something goes wrong. He defines a just culture as one that treats mistakes as products of faulty systems rather than individual failings, and notes this does not remove accountability. Drawing on Etsy, Atlassian and Brene Brown, he offers ground rules such as assuming good intentions, focusing on facts, identifying causes rather than culprits and staying consistent. His method has three steps: recap the event factually, reflect on behaviors and root causes using the five whys, and improve by choosing quick and structural wins with owners and deadlines. He recommends an external facilitator and "I" statements to keep the conversation from sliding back into blame.
points: A blameless postmortem moves the question from who caused the problem to what went wrong and why the system allowed it.
Blameless does not mean unaccountable, because teams that own their mistakes together learn from them and take more responsibility.
Ground rules include assuming good intentions, focusing on facts, identifying causes not culprits and applying the process consistently.
The process runs in three steps: recap the facts, reflect on behaviors and root causes, and improve through concrete actions.
Leaders should distinguish proximate from root causes and use the five whys to reach the point where one change prevents a whole class of incidents.
quotes: The underlying belief of a blameless culture is that mistakes are generally a product of faulty organizational cultures rather than the fault of one or more individuals.
A blameless culture doesn't mean a lack of accountability. On the contrary, when teams own their mistakes, they learn from them, increasing ownership and responsibility.
In a just culture, people ask, "What went wrong?" versus "Who caused the problem?
Root causes are reasons at the optimal place in the chain of events where making a change would prevent the entire class of incidents.
Even if someone did something that directly led to an incident, instead of asking, "Why did (name) do this?" ask, "Why did the system allow/ encourage them to do this?
Quick wins can build momentum and remove unnecessary pain, while structural wins require more time and resources but will prevent costly and significant incidents from happening.
